items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Finally I came up with Snooky Young... I called Snooky’s family... So he came in. I introduced him to Aaron... We came to work every day... We were just – we had to be models

ctx.x: Huh? Yeah, the actress and dancer. We became like families. I had my wife come out to California for the first time, and we stayed at Gerald and Etta’s. I had a band to meet her at the airport. That was fun. So I’ve know Gerald for quite a long time. As a matter of fact, just very recently, we had an occasion to play the Berne festival in Berne, Switzerland. Gerald came over and performed Lunceford tunes with Jon Faddis’s Carnegie Hall band. Gerald and Snooky Young are the only two living members of the old…

items.title: Clark Terry interviewed by Joe Williams and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, May 19, 1995
items.q: I had Snooky Young while we were in St. Louis. Snooky and I were roommates

ctx.x: Roommates. Sonny Payne, when I joined the Basie band, because I had a lot of roommates. I had Snooky Young while we were in St. Louis. Snooky and I were roommates and we shared a bathroom with Melba Liston, who had the next, she had like the adjoining door and the bathroom on her side and on our side.

items.title: Snooky Young and Gerald Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...Clark Terry was there... [INTERVIEWEE] Well they came out here see, that band started there.

ctx.x: He has recorded frequently with numerous bands and as a leader of his own small group.

Gerald Wilson was also born in 1919, in Shelby, Mississippi and played trumpet with Detroit’s Plantation Club Orchestra in 1936 which led to a three year engagement with Jimmie Lunceford. He performed in LA with Benny Carter and Les Hite, later doing a stint in the Army where he was able to continue his music with fellow soldiers Clark Terry, Ernie Royal and Willie Smith. Gerald’s composing and arranging skills began to gain attention and he led his first big band from 1944-47 with Snooky Young and Melba Liston…
Count Basie employed Gerald as an arranger and trumpet man from 1948-49.

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: "Here Snooks. Take this." It’s something that’s a little too difficult. They don’t want to work quite that hard... so they would . . .

ctx.x: Yeah, absolutely. Absolutely. We couldn’t have a speck on our trousers. We couldn’t have a wrinkle in the clothes. We couldn’t have a dirty shirt. We couldn’t wear filthy clothing. We had to be immaculate at all times. On time. If we hit at 4 o’clock in the afternoon, we’re sitting in our chairs at quarter to 4, ready to hit. And if somebody – which usually happened – ran into a piece of music that was too difficult, “Here, Clark. Here. Take this. Here Snooks. Take this.” It’s something that’s a little too…

Let me ask you this: since the representation was made to you, that we can’t find any musicians, when you got there, what did you find in terms of the level of musicianship? And how did it – when you compare them to your peers in the jazz world, what conclusion did you draw?
